title: The Harlem race riots of 1933 and 1943
summary: Butler describes LaGuardia calming the riots, looting of pawn shops, police horses slipping on marbles, and how the riots pushed entertainment downtown, starting with the Cotton Club.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Then when the race riots started happening, and LaGuardia started saying -- he was--(loved him) because LaGuardia loved him. He loved everybody. He come up there with his fireman hat on and he say, "please, please do not fight no more." And everybody, all of a sudden -- downtown was beautiful.
Now, you were here when that happened?

The first and the second one. Because, you see, downtown was reserved for the European man. Uptown, Harlem, you sit around 110th Street where you/get beat up and all kinds of things, you know, everybody wants to have fun. But after the race riot, everybody starts working downtown, socializing downtown. And that's the way what happened. And then, they decided to move everything downtown. The Cotton Club started the move downtown. Everything moved down, that's what happened.
Now, where were you -- when was the first one that you --
The first one, I think happened around '33. '33. I was working at the Arcadia Ballroom, and the second one was when everybody -- then everybody became happy.
I think it was '43 -- during the war.
Yeah, yeah. Then after that, everything was pretty. Broadway was lovely, then.
Could you describe the two of them as you recall them, what you were doing, what you saw?

Well, see, it wasn't ---see, race riots, see, there's some sections you don't see nothing about it. And some places everything was happening. So what I would see -- I was working on Broadway and I'd catch the 8th Avenue train, I'd be coming home, see. And they lasted about a day and a half, something like that. And what was happening, there would be -- first, they'd hit the pawn shops, seems they were always mad at the pawn shops. They'd tear them up and they'd tear the drug stores up, they'd tear the shoe stores up, everything like that. Everything was taken out of them. Then they'd be going downtown doing ugly things, and that's what was happening. There would be spasmodic things here and there, people getting hurt and police were coming up on their horses. And they'd put marbles on the streets and the horses would slip on them.
That was an awful thing to see. Broke their leg and they'd be shot dead.
You know, like you shoot marbles. The horse would get hurt.

There were a lot of slick things we were doing, man. And they had --home boy, whom they didn't know was a home boy, guys like Yellow Car/ (PHONETIC) and all these people. Yellow Car/would go (unintelligible) "Now, don't you bother this -- you fellows stop that now." And he'd get next to the cop and take his gun and take him around the corner and beat him, beat him to death. "Don't you bother this -- you know, I've got this shop up here." (Inaudible).

You see, anytime something -- things like doing two minute things to something white in America, they're going to stop that. They going to let him alone, see. They're going to let him alone. They love to see other people's blood be flowing, but when this other man says, well, I want his mother to do a bit of crying too (audible). That's what happened.
